title: Counting in stages
objectives: Count multi-stage outcomes with the multiplication rule.
Count ordered choices without repeats using factorials.

screens.prose: A set lunch is one starter followed by one main. The kitchen offers 3 starters and 4 mains. Each path through the tree, from the left to a leaf on the right, is one meal.

state.caption: One path from the left to the right is one meal

screens.question: Tap every complete meal, one leaf at a time, to count them.

hints.text: A meal ends at a main on the far right. How many mains hang off Soup?
Soup alone leads to 4 meals.
Each of the 3 starters leads to the same 4 mains. Tap all 12 leaves.

feedback.correct: Twelve meals: every starter goes with every main.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap each leaf on the far right once, under every starter.

byKey.starters: You tapped the 3 starters. A meal is a whole path, so tap the mains at the far right.
byKey.s: You tapped the Soup branch itself. Tap the mains to its right instead: each is one meal.
byKey.l: You tapped the Salad branch itself. Tap the mains to its right instead: each is one meal.
byKey.p: You tapped the Pâté branch itself. Tap the mains to its right instead: each is one meal.

explain.text: You tapped 3 groups of 4 leaves, one group per starter. That is $3 \times 4 = 12$ meals. Seven dishes make twelve meals, because each starter is paired with every main.

screens.prose: The same menu as a table: each row is a starter, each column a main, and each cell one meal. Move the sliders to change the menu.
screens.question: Start at 3 starters and 4 mains. Add one starter. How many new meals appear?

options.why: You added one dish. But the new starter pairs with every main, so it brings a whole row.
You counted the starters. The new row holds one meal per main, and there are 4 mains.
That doubles the menu. One more starter adds one row, not a copy of the table.

hints.text: Set Starters to 4 and watch the table. What appears?

feedback.correct: The new starter brings a full row of 4 meals.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Move Starters from 3 to 4 and count the cells in the new row.

byKey.one: You added one dish. But the new starter pairs with every main, so it brings a whole row.
byKey.twelve: That doubles the menu. One more starter adds one row, not a copy of the table.

explain.text: The fourth starter adds a row, and the row has one cell per main. So the count goes from $3 \times 4 = 12$ to $4 \times 4 = 16$. Each choice at one stage multiplies the choices at the other.

screens.prose: Multiplying the choices at each stage is the **multiplication rule**. It works whenever every choice at one stage leaves the same number of choices at the next. Now the lunch adds a dessert: tart or ice cream.

state.caption: Only the Soup branch is drawn in full

screens.question: How many three-course meals are there?

hints.text: Count the leaves under Soup first.
Soup leads to 4 mains, and each main splits into 2 desserts.
Soup gives $4 \times 2 = 8$ meals. Salad and Pâté give 8 each as well.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the meals under Soup, then remember the other two starters.

byKey.added: You added the dishes, $3 + 4 + 2$. Each meal is a path, and the paths multiply.
byKey.plus-two: You added 2 desserts to 12 meals. Each old meal splits into 2, so the count doubles.
byKey.soup: That is the Soup branch only. Salad and Pâté lead to 8 meals each as well.

explain.text: Under Soup there are $4 \times 2 = 8$ meals, and each starter has the same 8. So the rule gives $3 \times 4 \times 2 = 24$. Adding a stage multiplied the count by its 2 choices.

screens.prose: Five horses, A to E, run a race. A forecast names the 1st, 2nd and 3rd horse in order. A horse cannot finish in two places.

state.caption: Only A first, then A–B, is drawn in full

screens.question: How many different forecasts are possible?

hints.text: How many horses could finish 1st? Once that is fixed, how many could finish 2nd?
After A wins, only 4 horses are left for 2nd.
5 choices for 1st, then 4 for 2nd, then 3 for 3rd. Multiply.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each place has one fewer horse to choose from than the place before.

byKey.repeats: You let a horse fill two places, $5 \times 5 \times 5$. Once a horse is placed, it is gone.
byKey.added: You added $5 + 4 + 3$. Each choice for 1st carries all of the later choices, so multiply.
byKey.unordered: You counted groups of 3 horses. A forecast also says who came 1st, 2nd and 3rd.

explain.text: The tree shows 5 branches, then 4 under A, then 3 under A–B. The second stage depends on the first, but always has 4 choices. So the rule still multiplies: $5 \times 4 \times 3 = 60$.

screens.prose: Now the forecast names all five places, 1st to 5th. The tree draws one branch in full at each stage.

state.caption: One branch per stage drawn in full

screens.question: In how many orders can the five horses finish?

hints.text: Count the branches at each stage of the drawn path.
The stages offer 5, 4, 3, 2 and then 1 choice.
Multiply $5 \times 4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the number of choices at each of the five stages.

byKey.added: You added $5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1$. The stages multiply, as before.
byKey.repeats: You let a horse finish in more than one place. Each stage has one fewer horse.
byKey.three: That stops after 3rd place. The last two places still give $2 \times 1$ orders.

explain.text: The drawn path offers 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1 choices. A product that runs down to 1 is a **factorial**: $5! = 5 \times 4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1 = 120$. Filling 3 places gave $5 \times 4 \times 3 = \tfrac{5!}{2!}$, the full product with the unused $2 \times 1$ divided out.

screens.prose: Back to the lunch menu. Late in the day the ice cream runs out. Every meal still has three courses, and tart is the only dessert left.

state.caption: Only the Soup branch is drawn in full

screens.question: How many three-course meals are there now?

hints.text: Does a dessert with only one choice split any path?
Each main now leads to exactly one dessert.
Multiply $3 \times 4 \times 1$.

feedback.correct: A stage with one choice multiplies by 1.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each meal from the two-course menu now gets one dessert, the tart.

byKey.added: You added $3 + 4 + 1$. The stages still multiply.
byKey.plus-one: You added 1 for the tart. A forced choice extends each meal; it does not add a new one.
byKey.old: That still counts the ice cream. Only one dessert is left.
byKey.none: A stage with one choice still lets every meal through. Only a stage with no choices gives 0.

explain.text: Each of the 12 two-course meals gains the same tart, so no path splits. That is $3 \times 4 \times 1 = 12$. A stage with one choice multiplies by 1 and changes nothing.

canvas.caption: 12 meals, each ending in the tart

screens.prose: You roll a fair die and toss a fair coin. Sam says there are 6 faces and 2 sides, so 8 outcomes. Sam gives the chance of a 6 and heads as $\tfrac{1}{8}$.
screens.question: What is the chance of a 6 and heads?

options.why: You added 6 faces and 2 sides. Each face splits into 2 paths, so there are 12 outcomes.
You added $\tfrac{1}{6}$ and $\tfrac{1}{2}$. Both must happen, which is one path of 12.
That is the chance of a 6 alone. The coin then splits the 6 into two paths.

hints.text: Count the leaves at the bottom of the tree.
The 6 branch splits into heads and tails.
There are $6 \times 2 = 12$ equally likely paths. One of them is 6 then heads.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count every path, then count the paths that give a 6 and heads.

byKey.added: You added 6 faces and 2 sides. Each face splits into 2 paths, so there are 12 outcomes.
byKey.sum: You added the two chances. Both must happen, which is one path of 12.

explain.text: Sam counted 8 things, not 8 outcomes: an outcome is a whole path, a face and a side. Six faces each split into two sides, giving 12 equal paths. The 6 and heads is one of them, so the chance is $\tfrac{1}{12}$.

screens.prose: Each time, you multiplied the choices at every stage. If stage $i$ has $n_i$ choices, whatever came before, the count is this product. $$n_1 \times n_2 \times \cdots \times n_k$$ Filling $k$ places from $n$ items, no repeats, gives this count. $$n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1) = \frac{n!}{(n-k)!}$$ With $k = n$ the bottom is $0!$, and we set $0! = 1$.
screens.question: A desk names a lead trader and a different backup from 7 people. How many ways?

options.why: You let the same person be lead and backup. The backup must be one of the other 6.
You added the stage counts. Each lead goes with each of 6 backups, so multiply.
You treated lead and backup as the same job. Swapping them gives a different choice.

feedback.correct: Two stages, with 7 and then 6 choices: $\tfrac{7!}{5!} = 42$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the choices for lead, then for backup, then multiply.

explain.text: Lead has 7 choices and backup has the 6 people left. The rule multiplies them: $7 \times 6 = 42$. In factorials that is $\tfrac{7!}{5!}$, the full product with $5!$ divided out.

screens.prose: Forecasts of 3 places from $n$ horses gave $\tfrac{n!}{(n-3)!}$. Write $n!$ as its top three factors times the rest: $$\frac{n!}{(n-3)!} = \frac{n(n-1)(n-2)\,(n-3)!}{(n-3)!}$$ The top runs from $n$ down to 1, and below $n-2$ comes $(n-3)!$.
screens.question: Cancel the $(n-3)!$. What is left?

hints.text: The same factor sits on the top and the bottom.
Dividing $(n-3)!$ by itself leaves 1.
What remains is the three factors $n$, $n-1$ and $n-2$, multiplied.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Cancel the $(n-3)!$ on the top with the one on the bottom.

byKey.repeats: You wrote $n^3$, which lets a horse fill two places. Each stage has one fewer.
byKey.added: You added the three factors. The stages multiply.
byKey.unordered: You divided by the $3! = 6$ orders. A forecast keeps the order, so do not.

explain.text: Cancelling leaves $n(n-1)(n-2)$, the three stages you multiplied for the race. With $n = 5$ it gives $5 \times 4 \times 3 = 60$, your count. The factorial form is a short way to write that product.

screens.prose: An execution test sends a sequence of 4 trades, one leg after another. Each leg uses one of 6 instruments, and no instrument is traded twice. The order of the legs matters for the test.
screens.question: How many different 4-leg sequences can the test send?

hints.text: How many instruments could the first leg use? And the second?
Each leg removes one instrument from the pool.
The legs offer 6, 5, 4 and 3 choices. Multiply them.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the choices for each leg in turn, one fewer each time, and multiply.

byKey.repeats: You let an instrument appear twice, $6^4$. Each leg has one fewer to choose from.
byKey.unordered: You counted sets of 4 instruments. The legs are in order, so each set gives 24 sequences.
byKey.added: You added $6 + 5 + 4 + 3$. Each first leg carries all of the later choices, so multiply.
byKey.orders: You counted the orders of one set of 4 instruments. There are also 15 sets to choose from.

explain.text: Leg 1 has 6 instruments, leg 2 has 5 left, then 4, then 3. So there are $6 \times 5 \times 4 \times 3 = 360$ sequences, which is $\tfrac{6!}{2!}$. A test that tried each one at a minute a run would take six hours.

canvas.caption: One of the 360: Gold, FTSE, Bund, GBP

ideas: When every choice at one stage leaves the same number at the next, multiply the stage counts.
Without repeats each stage has one fewer choice: $n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1) = \dfrac{n!}{(n-k)!}$.
A stage with one choice multiplies by 1, and $0! = 1$ keeps $\dfrac{n!}{0!} = n!$.

formula.name: Multiplication rule
formula.note: Each $n_i$ counts the choices at stage $i$, whatever happened before.

summary.trap: Adding the stage counts (3 + 4 = 7) counts dishes, not meals. An outcome is a whole path.

quiz.prose: A login code is either 4 lower-case letters (26 choices each) or 8 digits (10 choices each). Characters may repeat.
quiz.question: Which kind of code has more possibilities?

options.why: You compared the alphabets. Each extra character multiplies the count, and 8 characters beat 4.
You multiplied length by alphabet size. Each character is a stage, so raise the alphabet size to the length.

feedback.correct: Length multiplies again with every character.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each character is a stage: multiply its choices once per character.

explain.text: Four letters give $26 \times 26 \times 26 \times 26 = 456{,}976$ codes. Eight digits give $10^8 = 100{,}000{,}000$, over 200 times as many. Each extra character multiplies the count, so length beats alphabet size.

quiz.prose: Four stocks can be ranked in $4! = 24$ orders. The formula $\tfrac{n!}{(n-k)!}$ with $n = k = 4$ gives $\tfrac{4!}{0!}$.
quiz.question: What value must $0!$ take for the formula to give 24?

byKey.zero: With $0! = 0$ the formula would divide by zero. It must be the value that leaves 24 unchanged.

explain.text: We need $\tfrac{24}{0!} = 24$, so $0! = 1$. That is a choice made so the formula works when every place is filled. It also fits: there is exactly one way to arrange nothing.

quiz.prose: An analyst ranks her top 3 picks, in order, from a watchlist of 8 stocks. No stock appears twice.
quiz.question: How many different rankings are possible?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the choices for 1st, 2nd and 3rd, one fewer each time.

byKey.repeats: You let a stock take two places, $8^3$. Each place has one fewer stock.
byKey.unordered: You counted sets of 3 stocks. A ranking also orders them, 6 ways per set.

explain.text: First place has 8 choices, second has 7, third has 6. The rule multiplies them: $8 \times 7 \times 6 = 336$, or $\tfrac{8!}{5!}$.

quiz.prose: You toss a fair coin and roll two fair dice.
quiz.question: What is the chance of heads and a double six? Give a fraction.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count every outcome of the three stages, then the ones you want.

byKey.added: You added $2 + 6 + 6 = 14$. The three stages multiply to 72 outcomes.
byKey.no-coin: That is a double six alone. The coin splits each roll into two outcomes.
byKey.one-die: That uses only one die. Both dice must show a six.

explain.text: The coin, the first die and the second die are three stages: $2 \times 6 \times 6 = 72$ equally likely outcomes. Heads, 6, 6 is one of them. So the chance is $\tfrac{1}{72}$.
